Needs: a copy of the facsimile (Marshall Item 611) to identify the letter and its original. If it is veiled plain language with no cipher groups, as the guide says, the right verdict is not_cipher and the entry is a removal candidate.

787.unvetted: Cipher texts not seen and the painting is not named. Sheldon, The Friedman Collection: An Analytical Guide (2014), Wayback PDF, text extracted and read at the item (Item 1040): 'Photographic copy of a painting by the German painter Winterhalter, on which is a series of cipher texts never deciphered. WFF has spent a few hours in an attempt to solve the cipher texts ... without success. The copy was given to him by Brig. Tiltman', with an extract of Vizetelly, Court Life of the Second French Empire, pp. 70-75. I opened Vizetelly 1908 (archive.org cu31924014604148, pp. 70-75): the pages describe the Empress Eugenie's household (Princess d'Essling, Duchess de Bassano, the Ladies of the Palace) and say nothing of a painting or a cipher; the only 'cyphers' in the book are the Emperor's codes (unrelated). The extract therefore points to Winterhalter's 'Empress Eugenie Surrounded by her Ladies in Waiting' (1855, Compiegne) as the painting, as an inference only. Searches 9 Nov 2026: 'Winterhalter painting cipher inscriptions undeciphered Tiltman Friedman Vizetelly'; 'Winterhalter Empress Eugenie Surrounded by her Ladies in Waiting cipher OR cryptogram inscription'; 'Friedman Tiltman Winterhalter painting photograph cipher worksheets Marshall Foundation Item 1040': no source mentions cipher text on any Winterhalter canvas, and none on the Compiegne picture. known.py 'Winterhalter': sweep README only. Needs: the photograph in Marshall Item 1040 (not online) to see the texts and confirm which painting.

834.unvetted: Not seen, and the two printed/parallel series that would hold the clear texts were not matched. Huntington finding aid (OAC, mssHooker Box 4, Folder 5 'Crossing the Potomac', 1862 Jan 20-Mar 5, creators R. B. Marcy and G. B. McClellan per the search result): 'Contains ciphered telegrams and a hand-drawn map of the lower Potomac.' It does not say how many telegrams, whether they are cipher-word copies or the operator's translations, or whether the clear text is written on them. The collection note (search result) says many of the papers are printed in the Official Records, and OR I.5 and I.51/1 print Marcy's and McClellan's telegrams to Hooker at Budd's Ferry for Feb 1862 in clear (search hits for 13 and 23 Feb 1862; the OR pages themselves were not opened), so the plaintext of these messages may already be in print; without item dates I could not match them. The Huntington's Eckert ledgers (mssEC; catalogue 648, targets/eckert1862) are the parallel series that could hold the same messages in cipher and clear, and were not checked. Searches 9 Nov 2026: 'Hooker January February 1862 cipher telegram lower Potomac crossing McClellan in cipher Official Records Budd's Ferry'; 'Huntington Library Joseph Hooker military papers Crossing the Potomac ciphered telegrams 1862'. known.py 'Hooker': own rows and sweep READMEs only. Needs: scans or an item list of Box 4 Folder 5, then a match against OR I.5/I.51 and the Eckert ledgers.
